Mental health

Psychosis

Hallucinations, delusions and schizophrenia: what they are, how they are treated and why early intervention matters.

Medical review Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Need help now? In Spain, 024 is free and open 24 hours; in an emergency call 112. Elsewhere, contact your local helpline or emergency services. This text is for general information: it cannot diagnose and does not replace seeing a professional. Where to get help →

What it is

Psychosis is a state in which a person partly loses contact with shared reality. Its main symptoms are:

  • Hallucinations: perceiving something that is not there, above all hearing voices.
  • Delusions: firm beliefs that do not match reality and do not change in the face of contrary evidence, such as feeling persecuted or watched.
  • Disorganised thinking and speech.
  • Sometimes negative symptoms: lack of motivation, withdrawal, reduced emotional expression.

Psychosis can occur in schizophrenia (which affects around 0.3–0.7% of people over their lifetime), in bipolar disorder, in severe depression, from drug use (potent cannabis, stimulants), from medical illnesses or from medicines. It usually first appears between late adolescence and age 30.

What it is not

Schizophrenia is not having a "split personality". People with psychosis are not, in general, violent: they are more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators. Many people occasionally hear voices without having a disorder, for example when falling asleep or while grieving.

How it is assessed

A first episode needs urgent specialist assessment to rule out medical causes (blood tests, sometimes brain imaging) and substance use. There is often an earlier phase of weeks or months with withdrawal, falling performance, suspiciousness or odd ideas.

Which interventions are studied

  • Early intervention programmes for first episodes: teams combining medication, psychotherapy, family support and help with study or work. They improve outcomes.
  • Antipsychotics: reduce positive symptoms and relapses. The lowest effective dose is sought and metabolic side effects are monitored.
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis and family interventions, which reduce relapse.
  • Supported employment and physical health care: stopping smoking, exercise, diet.
  • Clozapine is the treatment of choice when other antipsychotics have not worked.

How to seek help

For a first episode, see the family doctor or go to A&E; don't wait for it to "pass". If there is risk to the person or others, call emergency services (112 in Spain and across the EU).

How to support someone

Speak calmly and simply. Don't argue about the content of the delusions or play along: show that you understand their fear or distress. Family associations offer very valuable training and support.

Myths to avoid

  • "People with schizophrenia never recover". Many achieve a good personal and social recovery, especially with early and continued treatment.
  • "It's the family's fault". Old theories that blamed mothers have been discarded.
  • "Cannabis helps calm psychosis". On the contrary, it worsens the outlook.

References

  1. McCutcheon, R. A., Reis Marques, T. y Howes, O. D. (2020). Schizophrenia—an overview. JAMA Psychiatry, 77(2), 201–210.
  2. Correll, C. U. et al. (2018). Comparison of early intervention services vs treatment as usual for early-phase psychosis. JAMA Psychiatry, 75(6), 555–565.
  3. Di Forti, M. et al. (2019). The contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe (EU-GEI). The Lancet Psychiatry, 6(5), 427–436.
  4. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2014). Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management (CG178). Londres: NICE.
